name: Broad mite
summary: A microscopic tarsonemid mite reported from Cannabis and described by extension sources on hemp, but recent peer-reviewed reviews found no traceable primary evidence demonstrating its damage phenotype on hemp. Confirm the organism on plant-linked fresh growth; puckering, bronzing, stunting, or bud distortion alone remain unvalidated symptom transfer rather than Cannabis ground truth.
affectedParts: both surfaces of fresh expanding leaves
adjacent asymptomatic fresh growth used for repeat sampling
indicators: Plant-linked microscopy of protected fresh growth shows extremely small oval-to-round mites rather than relying on canopy distortion alone
Clear oval eggs with raised pale or white dots are attached to sampled leaf undersides or protected tissue and remain linked to the photographed plant
Adult females may show a lengthwise pale dorsal stripe, while organism color is treated cautiously because lighting and preparation alter appearance
Mites or characteristic eggs occur in the youngest expanding tissue, leaf undersides, axils, tips, buds, or shaded crevices where extension sources direct scouting
Warped, puckered, hardened, cupped, or strap-like young leaves occur on the same plant as compatible organisms, but the morphology remains supporting rather than causal evidence
Bronze, copper, or dark discoloration is concentrated on young protected tissue and is documented under neutral repeatable light
Serial images link short internodes or slowed growing tips to continued organism recovery rather than to cultivar architecture or one-time stress
Deformed or aborted flower buds remain connected to repeated plant-linked mite evidence and exclusion of thrips, russet mites, pathogens, and environmental injury
exclusions: Cigar-shaped mites with only two pairs of legs are present, supporting hemp russet mite rather than broad mite
Fine webbing, round eggs, and two-spotted mites are present, supporting spider-mite injury
Smooth colorless eggs and compatible cyclamen-mite morphology are present; dotted broad-mite eggs are not recovered
Thrips, shed skins, feeding scars, and dark fecal spots explain the damaged expanding tissue
Only older leaves follow a mobile-nutrient symptom pattern while protected new growth remains free of compatible organisms
Injury maps to the brightest or hottest canopy surface and measured PPFD or leaf temperature explains the distribution
Distortion follows a documented plant-growth-regulator herbicide, spray, pruning, rubbing, or other exposure pattern

Repeat plant-linked sampling of fresh adjacent growth, both leaf surfaces, axils, tips, and buds finds no compatible mites or dotted eggs and an independently confirmed alternative explains the syndrome

progression.description: Microscopy recovers compatible oval mites or dotted eggs from protected fresh growth. Organism detection establishes presence, not yet causal injury or severity.

Extension-described puckering, cupping, hardening, bronzing, or strap-like expansion appears on the same plant while compatible organisms remain detectable; the phenotype is not validated by a controlled Cannabis causal study.

Serial capture may show shorter internodes or slower tips with continued organism recovery, but cultivar, root-zone, nutrient, virus, viroid, thrips, spray, and environmental alternatives must remain open.
Bud deformation or abortion is documented with plant-linked organisms and an exclusion workup; flower morphology by itself must never be assigned to broad mite.

Old distorted tissue can persist after mites move or are no longer detected, so response is evaluated on marked subsequent growth and repeated fixed-site sampling rather than apparent recovery of old leaves.

lookAlikes: Copper, zinc, or other micronutrient disorder
Extreme-pH, high-EC, hypoxia, or other root-zone disorder
Beet curly top virus, phytoplasma, or another systemic pathogen
Cultivar-typical compact growth or leaf shape
Mechanical injury to the growing point
confirmation: Do not confirm broad-mite injury from curl, puckering, bronzing, stunting, bud distortion, one photograph, or one video; cap image/video-only confidence at 0.30 and route every proposed positive label to human review.
Capture plant ID, cultivar, stage, dates, whole-plant distribution, marked growing points, both surfaces of fresh leaves, axils, tips, and buds under neutral light before removing samples.

Inspect fresh expanding tissue adjacent to the worst damage at 20× or greater and with a dissecting microscope when available; retain scale-calibrated organism and egg images linked to the plant and sampling site.
Confirm compatible oval adults or clear oval eggs bearing raised pale dots; treat a female pale dorsal stripe as supporting morphology rather than a stand-alone character.
Separate broad mite from cigar-shaped two-pair-legged russet mites, web-producing spider mites with round eggs, smooth-egg cyclamen mites, and thrips using morphology or qualified taxonomic review.

Repeat fixed-site sampling across affected and apparently healthy plants because injury may lag behind feeding and damaged tissue may remain abnormal after mites move; a negative sample is not proof of absence.

Record root-zone pH, EC, water status, temperature, PPFD, leaf temperature, sprays, growth regulators, propagation source, and inspect for pathogens or nutrient disorders before assigning causal injury.
immediateActions: Quarantine suspect plants and stop moving cuttings or shared tools into clean areas while preserving representative plant-linked samples.
Microscope-screen neighboring plants and propagation material before choosing any control.
Retain untreated comparison tissue when lawful and practical so organism recovery and subsequent growth can be evaluated without confusing simultaneous interventions.
correctivePlan: Use only controls legal for the crop, jurisdiction, and growth stage, following the current label.
Track mites or eggs on fixed fresh-growth sampling sites; do not judge response from old distorted leaves.
Remove severely infested material without spreading mites and sanitize shared tools between plants.
prevention: Include protected new-growth sites in routine scouting rather than inspecting only mature fan leaves.
warnings: Leaf distortion, bronzing, short internodes, or bud deformation alone are not diagnostic, and no controlled Cannabis study cited here validates a universal broad-mite symptom sequence or threshold.

Utah State Extension describes broad-mite damage on hemp, while the USDA/University of Florida synthesis found no traceable published or observed evidence demonstrating broad-mite damage to hemp; this conflict requires plant-linked organism confirmation and human review.

The Pulkoski and Burrack experiment tested two-spotted spider mites and green peach aphids, not broad-mite feeding; its general piercing-sucking injury context cannot be relabeled as broad-mite causal evidence.
The two media assets below show the organism without a host and are morphology references, not Cannabis symptom ground truth.
Although their licenses permit reuse, both remain reference-only and excluded from automated training pending a separate training and dataset-split review.
No article or extension figure was copied in this enrichment; item-level automated-training rights and plant-linked Cannabis confirmation were not established.

sources.title: Broad Mite
sources.organization: Utah State University Extension, Utah Plant Pest Diagnostic Laboratory
supportedClaims: Broad mite (Polyphagotarsonemus latus) is documented on hemp and occupies shaded, protected leaf surfaces and crevices.
Adults are extremely small, oval to round, and light yellow to green; eggs are laid on leaf undersides.
Feeding can produce malformed, warped, or hardened young leaves and flower buds, bronzing, stunting, and aborted growth.

sources.title: Assessing the impact of piercing-sucking pests on greenhouse-grown industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press for the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: Broad mites are recognized among the most significant piercing-sucking pests of greenhouse-grown hemp.

Piercing-sucking pest injury in hemp can overlap visually with cupping, yellowing, leaf loss, and reduced reproductive performance, so pest presence must be confirmed rather than inferred from canopy symptoms.

sources.title: Broad Mite
supportedClaims: Broad mites prefer young, protected tissue and may no longer be present on the most damaged tissue because visible injury can persist after feeding.
Clear oval broad-mite eggs have raised pale dots, while cyclamen-mite eggs are smooth and russet mites have a narrow, conical body form.
Broad-mite injury can resemble plant-growth-regulator herbicide injury, nutrient problems, and other abiotic disorders; inspection at about 20× or by microscope is recommended.

sources.title: Arthropod and mollusk pests of hemp, Cannabis sativa (Rosales: Cannabaceae), and their indoor management plan in Florida
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press on behalf of the Entomological Society of America
supportedClaims: The Florida survey and literature synthesis reported Polyphagotarsonemus latus among organisms associated with hemp but found no published literature, personal observation, or communication demonstrating broad-mite damage to hemp.

The authors distinguish organism occurrence from the ability to reproduce, complete a life cycle, and damage hemp; a regional list or organism-only image is not evidence that a photographed plant syndrome was caused by broad mite.
The article presents broad-mite organism images at 10× and 30× for tentative field identification and recommends taxonomist consultation for species-level identification.
This evidence conflicts with treating extension symptom descriptions as experimentally validated Cannabis phenotypes and requires the uncertainty to remain attached to every symptom-led label.

sources.title: First Year Survey of Arthropods in California Hemp
supportedClaims: The 2021 California survey sampled eight hemp plots in Fresno and Ventura Counties every two weeks from August to mid-October using D-vac, leaf, and visual sampling.
Leaf collections specifically targeted hemp russet mite, two-spotted spider mite, and broad mite; ten leaves were collected at each of three random points per site and processed with a mite brush.

Very few mites were recovered overall and cannabis aphid was the only pest observed at noticeable density, so one negative inspection, one region, or one season cannot establish universal broad-mite absence or prevalence.
The survey did not establish a Cannabis broad-mite injury phenotype or causal symptom sequence; its sampling design is surveillance context rather than positive image ground truth.
